result.summary: Pindar celebrates Phylakidas of Aigina, youngest son of Lampon, for an Isthmian victory, counting it as the second libation of song after a Nemean win. He recalls the Aiakidai, especially Herakles' visit to Telamon, where an eagle signals the birth of Aias. He closes by praising Lampon's family and virtues.

scenes.summary: A modern note on the date and likely setting of the ode.

scenes.title: Second bowl of song
scenes.summary: Pindar likens the ode to a second mixed bowl for Zeus, Poseidon and the Nereids, wishes Lampon's family lasting glory, and invokes the Fates and the Aiakidai.
scenes.stakes: Hope of winning lasting renown before death or old age.

scenes.title: Aiakidai at Troy
scenes.summary: The fame of the Aiakidai spreads worldwide; Herakles with Telamon takes Troy and slays the Meropes and Alkyoneus.

scenes.title: Herakles' prayer and the eagle
scenes.summary: Herakles finds Telamon feasting and prays to Zeus that he have a son as staunch as the lion's hide. Zeus sends an eagle, and Herakles names the child Aias.
scenes.stakes: Telamon's hope for a brave son.

scenes.title: Praise of Lampon's house
scenes.summary: Pindar cuts the tale short and praises the victories of Phylakidas, Pytheas and Euthymenes, and Lampon's virtues, promising Dirke's holy water of song.

notable_quotes.reason: Pindar's view that toil and cost bring god-given excellence and fame, near the bounds of bliss.

analysis.text: Athletic victory is tied to heroic ancestry: the Aiakidai's deeds give glory to Aigina's present victors.
Epinikion was performed at banquets and paid for by victors' families; Pindar's brevity and moral praise (the 'just mean') reflect aristocratic values.

fun_facts.text: The eagle (aietos) in the tale is the folk-etymology for the name Aias.

language_notes.text: Mixing a bowl of wine was the opening of a banquet; Pindar compares each ode to a bowl mixed for a god, a toast in song.
Third bowls were traditionally poured to Zeus the Saviour; Pindar hopes for a third victory to honour him in song.
Klotho is one of the three Fates, who spin and fix a person's destiny; 'eld' means old age.
'Hundred-foot straight roads' means broad highways of fame; the Nile's springs and the Hyperboreans mark the world's far south and far north.
Herakles' sack of Troy punished Laomedon, who cheated him of promised horses; the Meropes are the people of Kos.
'Initiative libation' means pouring the first offering of wine to begin the feast.
The name Aias is linked to the Greek word for eagle, aietos, which is why the eagle sign prompts the naming.
'Argive fashion' implies a brief, compressed manner of speech; Pindar uses it to excuse cutting the tale short.
The Hesiod saying is probably that effort brings reward ('practice' is the key to success).
Dirke was Thebes' spring near Kadmos' gates; the Muses, daughters of Mnemosyne (Memory), made it spring, so it stands for Theban song.

context_notes.text: Nemea and Isthmos hosted athletic festivals; the lord of Isthmos is Poseidon, and the Nereids are sea nymphs, daughters of Nereus.
Peleus, father of Achilles, married the sea goddess Thetis; Telamon was father of Aias. Both belonged to the Aiakidai, Aigina's heroes.
The Nemean lion's skin, from Herakles' first labour, was impervious to weapons, which is why he wishes the child to be equally unyielding.
The pankration combined wrestling and boxing. The victors are Lampon's sons and their maternal uncle, of the Psalychidai clan of Aigina.

literary_notes.text: Casting anchor at the farthest bounds of bliss pictures lasting happiness as a ship reaching its final harbour.
The eagle, Zeus's bird, is a sign of divine consent and foreshadows the strength of Aias.
Pindar breaks off his myth, a typical device that returns attention to the victors and avoids excess.
Comparing Lampon to a Naxian whetstone among stones presents him as sharpening and surpassing other men.
The song is figured as holy spring water given to Lampon to drink, nourishing and honouring him.
